close_reason: Fixed in 9922e26: MemoryBackend::generate_invite_code now reads 16 bytes from getrandom (OS CSPRNG) and hex-encodes them — 128 bits of entropy, 32 chars wide. getrandom is gated behind the existing 'memory' feature so default builds are unchanged. Reference impl panics on OS-CSPRNG unavailability rather than degrading to a predictable fallback. New structural test asserts 256 distinct 32-char hex codes with low shared-prefix length — a behavioural canary the pre-fix timestamp impl could not satisfy. tests/common/mod.rs:136 kept as-is per the bead's option (c): it is already cfg(test)-equivalent (only exists in tests/) and never ships.
description:
Location: `crate-jmap-chat-server/src/memory.rs:517-527`

  fn generate_invite_code(&self) -> String {
      // test-only: not a CSPRNG
      format!(
          "{:012x}",
          std::time::SystemTime::now()
              .duration_since(std::time::UNIX_EPOCH)
              .unwrap_or_default()
              .as_nanos()
              & 0xffff_ffff_ffff,
      )
  }

CONCERN
The trait `ChatBackend::generate_invite_code` doc (`crate-jmap-chat-server/src/backend.rs:74-89`, fixed by closed JMAP-sc1b.78) instructs every implementor:

  /// Implementations MUST use a CSPRNG. `rand::rngs::OsRng` or the
  /// `getrandom` crate are the recommended choices.

But the reference implementation in this same crate's `memory.rs:517-527` uses nanosecond-since-epoch truncated to 48 bits. The inline comment labels it 'test-only: not a CSPRNG'.

Per workspace AGENTS.md and per the closed cookie-cutter findings (.82-.87 sweep), `MemoryBackend` is the **public reference implementation** that downstream operators copy-paste from — it is unconditionally compiled, publicly exported at `jmap_chat_server::memory::MemoryBackend`, and the canonical for the extension-server family per the workspace canonical-templates table. It is NOT `#[cfg(test)]`.

48 bits of nanosecond entropy against a known-second window is trivially brute-forceable: an attacker who knows roughly when an invite was created can enumerate ~10^9 candidate nanos in the window and submit Space/join requests with each. With current network throughput and no per-account rate limit on Space/join attempts (none in the handler), the entire window is searchable in minutes.

WHAT GOES WRONG
Key recovery — invite-code recovery → unauthorized Space membership for any space whose invite-creation time is roughly known.

The downstream-operator risk is the real concern: a deployment that starts from `MemoryBackend` as a scaffold (the AGENTS.md positions it as exactly this) and never overrides `generate_invite_code` ships a server with predictable invite codes. The inline 'test-only' comment is hedge-text; many operators will not read it.

PROPOSED FIX
Two options, in order of preference:

(a) Replace the impl with a CSPRNG:
        use rand::{rngs::OsRng, RngCore};
        let mut bytes = [0u8; 16];
        OsRng.fill_bytes(&mut bytes);
        hex::encode(bytes)
    Add `rand` (with `os_rng` feature) or `getrandom` to chat-server deps.

(b) Make the test-only nature unambiguous: `#[cfg(test)] fn generate_invite_code` and require the impl in non-test builds. This would break the 'use MemoryBackend as a scaffold' pattern but match the inline comment's stated intent.

(c) Apply the same change to `tests/common/mod.rs:136` (separate test-backend, also uses nanos) — that one can stay nanos with a clear cfg(test) gate.

ORACLE
- Closed JMAP-sc1b.78 — the trait-doc fix this finding is the matching reference-impl bug to.
- RFC 8620 §1.2 vs the ChatBackend doc — invite codes are explicitly secret-grade per the trait, distinct from generic JMAP Ids.

RISK CLASSIFICATION
P2. Predictable secret in the canonical reference backend that the workspace AGENTS.md positions for downstream copy-paste. Higher severity than .78 because .78 only fixed the doc; this is the matching code defect.
